nls_six_inch_first.attribution: Reproduced with the permission of the National Library of Scotland. Re-use terms for these particular layers are NOT established: NLS publish a per-layer re-use column, and the England and Wales six-inch and one-inch layers are not on it. Local and desktop use only — NLS ask that public websites use their Historic Maps API or contact them., county boundaries: This mapping made use of data provided by the Historic County Borders Project, https://www.county-borders.co.uk
nls_six_inch_first.note: The first edition is published county by county and the mosaics are NOT cut at the county line — they bleed over their neighbours. This layer is composited IN YOUR BROWSER: for each tile, every county covering it is fetched from the Library and masked to its own Historic Counties Standard polygon, so the whole of England and Wales draws at once with the seams on the boundaries. A pixel is taken only where the county owns the ground AND its own sheet has something to say there. Nothing below zoom 9, and the first pan over new ground is slow.

nls_ad_chart.label: Admiralty charts — 4 sheets
nls_ad_chart.attribution: Reproduced with the permission of the National Library of Scotland. Re-use terms for these particular layers are NOT established: NLS publish a per-layer re-use column, and the England and Wales six-inch and one-inch layers are not on it. Local and desktop use only — NLS ask that public websites use their Historic Maps API or contact them.
nls_ad_chart.note: Admiralty charts — the only source found that DRAWS the water rather than stopping at it, which is what makes them useful for adjudicating a dead end at tidal water. MEASURED COVERAGE, so nobody plans around them as general: of a sample of 400 seed nodes, 20% have a chart tile; of 400 other tidal termini, 14%. FOUR SEEDS IN FIVE HAVE NO CHART. Individual sheets, not a series: two charts over one tile is normal, they overlap and disagree, and they are UNDATED — the identifier is an accession number, not a year. A chart surveyed over an estuary that has since silted is evidence about a coast that no longer exists, so this is a backdrop for a person to look at and never a source for a rule. Stage 1 takes its tidal test from the survey's own form = tidalRiver.

thinning.note: Least length drawn, in metres, by zoom. A link shorter than this is not drawn UNLESS it belongs to a class that is never thinned.
never_thinned: in scope and not reaching tidal water — the defect
geometry this project added (origin is not 'survey')

historic_warning: A historic sheet under this network is a BACKDROP AND NOT EVIDENCE. Stage 1 is a modern river network and makes no historical claim whatever: nothing drawn on it is dated, and a channel lying over an 1890s sheet is not thereby attested in the 1890s. The backdrops are here to read the ground against, and for the stages that will make dated claims — not to let this one imply a claim it does not make. Re-use terms for these layers are not established and no sheet image may be published until they are.
_no_keys: EVERY BACKDROP HERE IS KEYLESS, AND THAT IS A PROPERTY OF THE FILE RATHER THAN A CONFIGURATION. The local viewer injects a key from a gitignored .env at request time; a published site has no server to do that, so a keyed entry could only work by shipping the key — and Pages is public even though the repository is not, so a published key can be rotated but never withdrawn. The keyed options are therefore removed from this copy rather than left present and disabled: an entry that can only ever fail is an invitation to make it work. Dropped here: carto_dark, carto_light, nls_six_inch_maptiler.
_labels: Generated labels show the Library's own tileset identifier verbatim in parentheses. A number in an identifier is not a date and must not be rendered as one: `air-photos-1250` is a scale of 1:1250, whose bucket siblings are 2500 and 10560, and it read as thirteenth-century beside an epoch selector. Only the hand-written labels carry dates, and those are claims someone can be held to.
